proposal: Among its cross-agency requests, the Mandate asks the State Department to quickly impose stiff sanctions on recalcitrant countries until they actually accept deportees, not merely promise to. It asks DOJ either to move the immigration courts to DHS or to treat immigration judges and Board of Immigration Appeals members as national security personnel, decertify their union, and hire significantly more. The same list also covers housing, education, labor, Treasury and intelligence items that this record does not track.

status_summary: Executive Order 14159, section 13 (signed 2025-01-20), directs State and DHS to apply INA section 243(d) visa sanctions to countries that refuse removable nationals; the Laken Riley Act (approved 2025-01-29) lets states sue the Secretary of State over a failure to apply them; and on 2025-04-05 the Secretary of State announced revocation of all visas held by South Sudanese passport holders and a halt to new issuance over South Sudan's failure to accept returns. For the immigration judges' union, the Federal Labor Relations Authority had already excluded immigration judges from their bargaining unit as management officials in 2020 and 2022, before this period; the only later step found is EO 14251 of 2025-03-27, which excludes the Department of Justice as a whole from the federal labor-management relations program without naming EOIR. The outcome of the judges' December 2024 petition to restore the union was not found, and no step moving EOIR to DHS was found. On 2025-08-28 EOIR published a final rule letting the Director designate any attorney as a temporary immigration judge for renewable terms of up to six months. A March 2026 CRS Insight reports that permanent immigration judge numbers fell from 735 at the end of FY2024 to 557 at the end of the first quarter of FY2026, while EOIR announced 25 temporary judges in October 2025 and 27 more in February 2026; the same Insight notes that Public Law 119-21 funds immigration judge hiring and sets a ceiling of not more than 800 judges from 2028-11-01. A significant increase in permanent hiring was not found.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14159 was signed; section 13 directs the Secretaries of State and Homeland Security to apply INA section 243(d) sanctions where appropriate and to remove barriers to prompt returns, weighing delayed identity confirmation.

The Laken Riley Act (Public Law 119-1) was approved; section 3(c) adds a subsection to INA section 243 letting a state attorney general sue the Secretary of State for injunctive relief over a failure to discontinue visas as required by section 243(d).

Executive Order 14251 was signed, listing the Department of Justice as a whole among agencies excluded from the federal labor-management relations program; it does not name EOIR or immigration judges.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced revocation of all visas held by South Sudanese passport holders and a halt to further issuance, saying South Sudan's government had not fully accepted timely return of citizens the United States seeks to remove.

timeline.event: EOIR published a final rule, Designation of Temporary Immigration Judges (90 FR 41883, effective on publication), letting the Director, with Attorney General approval, designate any attorney as a temporary immigration judge for renewable terms of up to six months.

title: Sanction countries that refuse deportees; decertify the immigration judges' union
uncertainties: The page 167 list is heterogeneous, so this record covers the sanctions item and the immigration judges' union item; the EOIR transfer is tracked in c05-01, the Labor wage-level item in c05-07 and the Intelligence Community item in c05-14, and the HUD, Education and Treasury items are not tracked and need their own research. The South Sudan statement was read through a hosted copy because state.gov did not load. A Cuban delegation visa denial reported in February 2026 under section 243(d) comes from a tracking site summary of a newspaper report and is not used. For the union element, the decertification events (FLRA 2020 and 2022) predate this period; the only event since 2025-01-20 is EO 14251's DOJ-wide exclusion, which does not name EOIR or immigration judges, and a search found no FLRA ruling on the December 2024 restoration petition. Whether any 2025 DOJ action treats judges as national security personnel was not found. A 2026-10-19 check found no FLRA or court action on the immigration judges' union or on EO 14251 as it touches EOIR in the sources reachable (results were from 2020 to 2022 or 2024), and no further 243(d) sanction announcement beyond South Sudan from a primary source; one low-quality aggregator article on 2026 country lists was not used. The CRS Insight was read through the everycrsreport.com mirror and its headcount stops at the end of the first quarter of FY2026 (2025-12-31); the temporary judge announcements of October 2025 and February 2026 are carried in the summary on the CRS account rather than as dated events because the EOIR announcements themselves were not opened. Whether designating temporary judges counts toward the hiring item is a judgment call; it adds adjudicators without raising the permanent corps.
